summary: Follow-up plan of layer CA.2 (sequences and generating functions) of the roadmap 'Classical arithmetic, sequences, polynomials and reciprocity'. It plans what the accepted first pass left open. Eulerian numbers A(n, q), counted by descents with A(0, 0) = 1, with their factorial sum, symmetry, recurrence, Worpitzky identity and unimodality, and the inequalities of Lawrence–Sawin's Appendix C (Lemmas C.1–C.5) at their exact ranges. Yu's binomial arithmetic: divisibility of generalised binomial coefficients by n/gcd(n, m), the p-free factorial f_p(N) with its factorial split and unit property, the factorisations of C(np, mp) and C(−np, mp) with the sign (−1)^{m(p−1)}, and the Luo–Zhu congruence f_p(p^αN) ≡ f_p(p^α)^N (mod p^{2α}) with the exceptional case p = 2, α = 1. Ward's strong divisibility theorem for elliptic divisibility sequences: the explicit curve E_{b,c,d} whose point (0, 0) carries normEDS b c d, the zero set over a field, the filtration E_k(ℚ_p) for an arbitrary integral equation, and strong divisibility at primes p ∤ W₂W₃ through Tau Ceti's multiplication formula for division polynomials; the primes dividing W₂W₃ and the singular attached curves remain a recorded gap. Three supplier lemmas close the remaining obligations of the first pass's review frontier: the formal derivatives of sine and cosine with sin² + cos² = 1, and the divergence of the Bernoulli and secant-plus-tangent series on and beyond their circles of convergence. The maximal divisor bound that AdditiveCombinatorics requested from this layer is AnalyticNumberTheory's node AN.5/divisor-maximal-order and is not planned here.

nodes.title: Eulerian numbers
nodes.statement: For n, q ∈ ℕ, the Eulerian number A(n, q) is the number of permutations σ of {1, …, n} with exactly q descents, a descent being a position i with 1 ≤ i < n and σ(i) > σ(i + 1). In Lean the permutations are Equiv.Perm (Fin n) and descentCount σ counts the positions i : Fin n with i + 1 < n and σ(i + 1) < σ(i). The empty permutation has no descent, so A(0, 0) = 1 and A(0, q) = 0 for q ≥ 1; for n ≥ 1, A(n, q) = 0 for q ≥ n. The count by ascents (σ(i) < σ(i + 1)) gives the same numbers. In Stanley's indexing A_Stanley(d, k) = A(d, k − 1) (his k counts 1 + des), and Lawrence–Sawin's A(n, q) is this A(n, q).
hypotheses: n and q are natural numbers; no range condition is built into the definition, the vanishing outside 0 ≤ q < n (n ≥ 1) is a theorem.

The zero-degree value A(0, 0) = 1 is the count of the empty permutation. It is kept separate from Lawrence–Sawin's convention 'A(n, q) = 0 unless 0 ≤ q < n', which they use only for n ≥ 1, and from Stanley's convention A_Stanley(0, k) = δ_{0k} (that is A₀(x) = 1), which is a separate normalisation of his shifted indexing at d = 0 and does not correspond to A(0, 0) under k = q + 1; the identities planned here (row sums, Worpitzky at m = q + 1 ≥ 1) hold with A(0, 0) = 1.
proofSteps: Define descentCount σ as the cardinality of the finite set of positions i : Fin n with i + 1 < n and σ(i + 1) < σ(i), and A(n, q) as the cardinality of {σ ∈ Equiv.Perm (Fin n) : descentCount σ = q}.
The basic identities (sum n!, symmetry, recurrence, Worpitzky) are proved in eulerian-basic-identities; this node fixes the object and its conventions.
acceptance: A(4, ·) = 1, 11, 11, 1 and A(5, ·) = 1, 26, 66, 26, 1 (Stanley's table of Eulerian polynomials).
A(0, 0) = 1, so the row sums are n! for every n ≥ 0, including n = 0.

nodes.title: Basic identities of Eulerian numbers
nodes.statement: For all n, q ∈ ℕ: (a) Σ_{q=0}^{n} A(n, q) = n!; (b) for q < n, A(n, q) = A(n, n − 1 − q); (c) A(n + 1, q + 1) = (q + 2)·A(n, q + 1) + (n − q)·A(n, q), with natural subtraction (for q ≥ n both sides vanish); (d) Worpitzky's identity (q + 1)ⁿ = Σ_{j=0}^{q} A(n, j)·C(n + q − j, n); (e) A(n, 0) = 1 and A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1; (f) the number of permutations with q ascents is A(n, q).
hypotheses: n, q ∈ ℕ; (b) needs q < n, which forces n ≥ 1.
proofSteps: (a) The sets {σ : des σ = q}, 0 ≤ q ≤ n, partition Equiv.Perm (Fin n), whose cardinality is n! (Fintype.card_perm).

(b) and (f): reversal σ ↦ σ ∘ rev sends a permutation with q descents to one with n − 1 − q descents, and complementation σ ↦ rev ∘ σ exchanges descents and ascents (Stanley p. 40, the paragraph before Proposition 1.4.3).

(c) Insert n + 1 into a permutation of [n]: inserting it into a descent slot or at the end keeps the descent number, inserting it into an ascent slot or at the front raises it by one; this is Stanley's recurrence (1.39) A(d + 1, k) = kA(d, k) + (d − k + 2)A(d, k − 1) with k = q + 2.

(d) For n ≥ 1, Stanley's Proposition 1.4.4 gives Σ_{m≥0} mⁿxᵐ = A_n(x)/(1 − x)^{n+1} with A_n(x) = Σ_j A(n, j)x^{j+1}; expanding 1/(1 − x)^{n+1} = Σ_k C(n + k, n)x^k (Mathlib's PowerSeries.invOneSubPow) and comparing coefficients of x^{q+1} gives (d). At n = 0 Stanley sets A₀(x) = 1 rather than x, so (d) is checked directly there: only j = 0 contributes, and both sides are 1 because A(0, 0) = 1.
(e) A(n, 0) = 1 because only the identity has no descent; A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1 follows from (d) at q = 1: 2ⁿ = A(n, 0)C(n + 1, n) + A(n, 1).
acceptance: Row 5 is 1, 26, 66, 26, 1, summing to 120 and symmetric.

nodes.title: Unimodality of the rows of Eulerian numbers
nodes.statement: For n ∈ ℕ and q with 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1: A(n, q) ≤ A(n, q + 1). With the symmetry A(n, q) = A(n, n − 1 − q), each row A(n, 0), …, A(n, n − 1) rises weakly to its middle and falls symmetrically after it.
hypotheses: 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 means q + 1 ≤ (n − 1)/2, the left half of the row; for n = 0 the hypothesis never holds.
proofSteps: Induction on n with the recurrence of eulerian-basic-identities (c): A(n, q + 1) − A(n, q) = (q + 2)A(n − 1, q + 1) + (n − 2q − 2)A(n − 1, q) − (n − q)A(n − 1, q − 1) for 1 ≤ q (and the analogous expression at q = 0).

Under 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 the index q + 1 is at most the middle (n − 2)/2 of row n − 1, or equals it up to the symmetric partner when n is odd; by the induction hypothesis and the symmetry, A(n − 1, q + 1) ≥ A(n − 1, q) ≥ A(n − 1, q − 1).
Hence the difference is at least ((q + 2) + (n − 2q − 2) − (n − q))·A(n − 1, q − 1) = 0, all coefficients other than the last being nonnegative because n − 2q − 2 ≥ 1.

Alternatively (Stanley, Exercise 1.50(e) with its solution): the Eulerian polynomial has only real zeros (Exercise 1.49), hence log-concave coefficients by Newton's inequalities, hence unimodal; symmetry places the peak in the middle.
acceptance: Checked numerically for every n ≤ 70 and every q in the range.

nodes.title: Power and factorial bounds for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemmas C.1–C.2)
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 and q ≥ 0: (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ (the left side computed in ℤ), and A(n, q) ≤ n!. The upper bound (q + 1)ⁿ and A(n, q) ≤ n! hold for n = 0 as well.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1 for the lower bound, as in the source; q ∈ ℕ arbitrary (for q ≥ n the bounds are consistent with A(n, q) = 0).
proofSteps: Upper bound: by Worpitzky's identity (eulerian-basic-identities (d)) (q + 1)ⁿ is a sum of nonnegative terms one of which is A(n, q)·C(n, n) = A(n, q). (Lawrence–Sawin's argument: labelling [n] by 1, …, q + 1 and listing each label class in decreasing order gives every permutation with at most q ascents.)

Lower bound (Lawrence–Sawin's argument): the labellings producing a permutation with fewer than q ascents have two adjacent labels whose classes are separated; recording the position j ∈ {0, …, n} of the cut and merging the labels injects them into (n + 1)·qⁿ data, so the number of permutations with exactly q ascents is at least (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ.
A(n, q) ≤ n! from Σ_q A(n, q) = n! (eulerian-basic-identities (a)).
Ascents and descents give the same numbers (eulerian-basic-identities (f)), so the source's ascent count is A(n, q).
acceptance: n = 3, q = 1: 2³ − 4·1 = 4 ≤ A(3, 1) = 4 ≤ 8: the lower bound is attained.
For q ≥ n the lower bound is ≤ 0, consistent with A(n, q) = 0 (checked for n ≤ 70, q ≤ n + 2).

nodes.title: Eulerian numbers with few descents (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.3)
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and q ∈ ℕ with q < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1 (natural logarithm, real comparison): (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2; the hypothesis on q is the real inequality q + 1 < n/(log(n + 1) + 1).
proofSteps: From 1/(q + 1) < log((q + 1)/q) for q ≥ 1, ((q + 1)/q)ⁿ > e^{n/(q+1)}; the hypothesis n/(q + 1) > log(n + 1) + 1 gives ((q + 1)/q)ⁿ > e(n + 1), that is (n + 1)qⁿ < (q + 1)ⁿ/e (trivially true at q = 0).
Insert this into the lower bound of eulerian-power-bounds: A(n, q) ≥ (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ > (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ; the upper bound is the upper half of that node.
acceptance: Checked numerically for n ≤ 70 and every admissible q.

nodes.title: A product inequality for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.4)
hypotheses: 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2, which forces n ≥ 5; for 3r − 2 ≥ n the right side is 0.
proofSteps: Small n: for n ≤ 20 the finitely many cases are checked by computation (the source's ancillary Python code, bound-B; rechecked here for all n ≤ 70).
Assume n ≥ 21 and r ≤ n/2 (for r > n/2, 3r − 2 ≥ n and the right side vanishes). There is an integer r₀ with √n ≤ r₀ < n/(log(n + 1) + 1), so either r < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) or r ≥ r₀.

If r < n/(log(n + 1) + 1): eulerian-small-descent-bounds gives A(n, r − 1) ≥ (1 − 1/e)rⁿ, and eulerian-power-bounds gives 2A(n, 3r − 2) ≤ 2(3r − 1)ⁿ; and (1 − 1/e)²r^{2n} > 2(3r − 1)ⁿ + (1 − 1/e)rⁿ for r ≥ 3, n ≥ 14.

If r ≥ r₀: by eulerian-unimodal A(n, r − 1) ≥ A(n, r₀ − 1) (r − 1 ≤ n/2 − 1 is in the rising half), and eulerian-small-descent-bounds at r₀ − 1 gives A(n, r₀ − 1)(A(n, r₀ − 1) − 1) > (3/10)r₀^{2n} ≥ (3/10)nⁿ > 2·n! ≥ 2A(n, 3r − 2) by eulerian-power-bounds (A ≤ n!).
acceptance: Checked numerically for every n ≤ 70 and 3 ≤ r ≤ n − 2.

nodes.title: The ratio A(n, 2)/A(n, 1)² (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.5)
proofSteps: eulerian-power-bounds gives A(n, 2) ≤ 3ⁿ, and for n ≥ 6 eulerian-small-descent-bounds at q = 1 gives A(n, 1) ≥ (1 − 1/e)2ⁿ (its hypothesis 1 < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1 holds from n = 6).
Hence 27A(n, 2)/A(n, 1)² ≤ 27(3/4)ⁿ/(1 − 1/e)², which is < 1 for n ≥ 15.
The cases 11 ≤ n ≤ 14 are checked directly from A(n, 1) = 2ⁿ − n − 1 and the recurrence (e.g. n = 11: A(11, 1) = 2036, A(11, 2) = 152 637, and 27·152 637 = 4 121 199 < 4 145 296).
acceptance: The inequality fails for 3 ≤ n ≤ 10 (checked), so the hypothesis n ≥ 11 cannot be weakened.
Checked numerically for n ≤ 70.

nodes.title: Divisibility of generalised binomial coefficients (Yu, Lemme 7.2.2)
nodes.statement: For a nonzero integer n and an integer m ≥ 1, n/gcd(n, m) divides the generalised binomial coefficient C(n, m) = n(n − 1)···(n − m + 1)/m! (Mathlib's Ring.choose on ℤ), negative upper entries included. The supporting absorption identity: for every n ∈ ℤ and m ∈ ℕ, (m + 1)·C(n, m + 1) = n·C(n − 1, m).
hypotheses: n ∈ ℤ, n ≠ 0; m ∈ ℕ, m ≥ 1. For m > n ≥ 1, C(n, m) = 0 and the statement is trivial.
proofSteps: Absorption: multiply both sides by m! and use Ring.descPochhammer_eq_factorial_smul_choose: (m + 1)!·C(n, m + 1) is the falling factorial n(n − 1)···(n − m) = n·[(n − 1)···(n − m)] = n·m!·C(n − 1, m); cancel m! in the torsion-free ℤ.
Write g = gcd(n, m), n = g·n′, m = g·m′ with gcd(n′, m′) = 1. Absorption at m − 1 gives m·C(n, m) = n·C(n − 1, m − 1), so m′·C(n, m) = n′·C(n − 1, m − 1) is divisible by n′.
Since gcd(m′, n′) = 1, n′ divides C(n, m) (Int.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right_of_gcd_one).
acceptance: n = −4, m = 2: C(−4, 2) = 10 and n/gcd = −2 divides it.
The gcd cannot be dropped: 4 ∤ C(4, 2) = 6.
Checked for every 0 < |n| ≤ 40 and 1 ≤ m ≤ 29.

nodes.title: The p-free factorial
nodes.statement: For a natural number p and N ∈ ℕ, the p-free factorial f_p(N) is the product of the integers 1 ≤ i ≤ N with p ∤ i; f_p(0) = 1 (empty product). For p prime, N! = p^{⌊N/p⌋}·⌊N/p⌋!·f_p(N) and f_p(N) is prime to p (a p-adic unit). Negative arguments are not part of the definition.
hypotheses: p, N ∈ ℕ; the factorial split holds for every p (for p = 0 and p = 1 it degenerates to N! = N! and N! = N!·1), while the unit property needs p prime.
proofSteps: Define f_p(N) := ∏ over i ∈ Icc 1 N with ¬ p ∣ i of i.
Factorial split: the multiples of p up to N are p·1, …, p·⌊N/p⌋, whose product is p^{⌊N/p⌋}·⌊N/p⌋!; the other factors give f_p(N) (Finset.prod_filter_mul_prod_filter_not).
Unit property: a product of integers prime to p is prime to p (Nat.Prime.coprime_iff_not_dvd and Nat.coprime_prod_left_iff).
acceptance: f_p(N) is not the prime-to-p part of N!: f_2(6) = 15 while 6! = 2⁴·45.

nodes.title: Binomial coefficients of multiples of p through the p-free factorial
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and f_p the p-free factorial. (a) For n ≥ m ≥ 0: C(np, mp)·f_p(mp)·f_p((n − m)p) = C(n, m)·f_p(np). (b) For n ≥ 1 and m ≥ 0, with generalised binomial coefficients: C(−np, mp)·f_p(mp)·f_p(np) = (−1)^{m(p−1)}·C(−n, m)·f_p(np + mp).
hypotheses: p prime; (a) n ≥ m ≥ 0; (b) n ≥ 1, m ≥ 0. The sign (−1)^{m(p−1)} matters only for p = 2.
proofSteps: (a) By the factorial split of p-free-factorial, (kp)! = p^k·k!·f_p(kp) for every k; substitute into C(np, mp) = (np)!/((mp)!((n − m)p)!) and cancel p^n = p^m·p^{n−m}.

(b) By Ring.choose_neg, C(−N, M) = (−1)^M·C(N + M − 1, M) for N ≥ 1; and C(N + M − 1, M) = C(N + M, M)·N/(N + M). Apply this to (N, M) = (np, mp) and to (n, m): the ratio C(−np, mp)/C(−n, m) is (−1)^{mp−m}·C((n + m)p, mp)/C(n + m, m), and (a) with (n + m, m) turns this into (−1)^{m(p−1)}·f_p((n + m)p)/(f_p(mp)f_p(np)).
acceptance: Checked for p ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7}, n < 9, m < 9.

nodes.title: The Luo–Zhu congruence for p-free factorials
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and α ≥ 1 with p odd or α ≥ 2. For every N ≥ 0: f_p(p^α·N) ≡ f_p(p^α)^N (mod p^{2α}). In the excluded case p = 2, α = 1: f_2(2N) ≡ (−1)^{⌊N/2⌋} (mod 4). The exclusion is necessary: f_2(4) = 3 ≢ 1 = f_2(2)² (mod 4).
hypotheses: p prime; α ≥ 1; p ≠ 2 or α ≥ 2 for the main congruence; N ∈ ℕ.
proofSteps: Induction on N; N = 0 is f_p(0) = 1. For the step, f_p(p^αN) = f_p(p^α(N − 1))·∏_{1 ≤ i ≤ p^α, p ∤ i}(p^α(N − 1) + i).
Modulo p^{2α} the product is f_p(p^α)·(1 + p^α(N − 1)·Σ_{i} i^{−1}), the inverses taken modulo p^{2α} (the cross terms carry p^{2α}).

Pair i with p^α − i: 1/i + 1/(p^α − i) = p^α/(i(p^α − i)), so p^α divides the sum of inverses. The pairing has no fixed point because p^{α−1}(p − 1), the number of units, is even and i = p^α/2 is not a unit (p odd, or p = 2 with α ≥ 2); for p = 2, α = 1 the sum is 1 and the argument fails.
Hence the factor is ≡ f_p(p^α) (mod p^{2α}) and the induction closes.
p = 2, α = 1: f_2(2N) is the product of the odd numbers below 2N, of which ⌊N/2⌋ are ≡ 3 (mod 4).
acceptance: Checked for p ∈ {3, 5, 7} with α ≤ 3, p = 2 with α ∈ {2, 3}, and N ≤ 11, and f_2(2N) mod 4 for N < 60; at p = 2, α = 1 the congruence fails exactly for N ≡ 2, 3 (mod 4) in that range.

nodes.title: The Weierstrass curve of a normalised elliptic divisibility sequence
nodes.statement: Let K be a field and b, c, d ∈ K with b ≠ 0, c ≠ 0. The curve E_{b,c,d} is the Weierstrass curve with a₁ = (d + b⁴)/(bc), a₂ = c/b², a₃ = b, a₄ = a₆ = 0, that is y² + ((d + b⁴)/(bc))xy + by = x³ + (c/b²)x². The point P = (0, 0) lies on it and is nonsingular (∂/∂y at P is a₃ = b ≠ 0), and the division polynomials of Mathlib evaluated at P are the normalised EDS: ψₙ(P) = normEDS b c d n for every n ∈ ℤ. Its discriminant is Δ(E_{b,c,d}) = −D(b, c, d)/(b⁴c³) with D(b, c, d) = d b¹² + (3d² − c³)b⁸ + (3d³ − 20c³d)b⁴ + 16c⁶ + 8c³d² + d⁴. The curve may be singular (Δ = 0); P is always a nonsingular point.
hypotheses: K a field; b ≠ 0 and c ≠ 0 (a nondegenerate sequence: W₂W₃ ≠ 0). In normEDS form W₄ = db, so W₂ | W₄ is built in.
No hypothesis on Δ: the identification ψₙ(P) = Wₙ is a polynomial identity and holds on singular cubics.
proofSteps: Compute at P: ψ₂(P) = 2·0 + a₁·0 + a₃ = b; Ψ₃(0) = b₈ = a₁²a₆ + 4a₂a₆ − a₁a₃a₄ + a₂a₃² − a₄² = (c/b²)·b² = c; preΨ₄(0) = b₄b₈ − b₆² = (a₁b)·c − b⁴ = d, since b₄ = 2a₄ + a₁a₃ = a₁b and b₆ = a₃² = b².

Mathlib defines ψₙ = normEDS ψ₂ (C Ψ₃) (C preΨ₄) n in R[X][Y] (WeierstrassCurve.ψ); evaluation at (0, 0) is the ring homomorphism Polynomial.evalEvalRingHom 0 0, and map_normEDS carries normEDS through it, giving ψₙ(P) = normEDS b c d n.
Nonsingularity: WeierstrassCurve.Affine.nonsingular_zero (P = (0, 0) is nonsingular iff a₆ = 0 and (a₃ ≠ 0 or a₄ ≠ 0)).

The discriminant formula is a direct computation of Δ = −b₂²b₈ − 8b₄³ − 27b₆² + 9b₂b₄b₆ (checked on the values below); D is Ward's discriminant polynomial as printed by Silverman–Stephens, Appendix A (31), up to the factor 2⁸3¹²b⁸c⁹ of their short model.
Base change: the coefficients are rational functions of b, c, d, so (E_{b,c,d}).map f = E_{f b, f c, f d} for a field homomorphism f.
acceptance: b = 1, c = −1, d = 1: a₁ = −2, a₂ = −1, a₃ = 1; the substitution y ↦ y + x turns it into y² + y = x³ − x (conductor 37), with Δ = 37, and the sequence is 0, 1, 1, −1, 1, 2, −1, −3, −5, 7, −4, … (Silverman, Example 1).
b = 2, c = 3, d = 2: Δ = 0 (a cusp: c₄ = 0 as well) and normEDS 2 3 2 = id (Tau Ceti normEDS_two_three_two_eq_id).

nodes.title: Division polynomials at a nonsingular point
nodes.statement: Let W be a Weierstrass curve over a field F (possibly singular) and P = (x, y) a nonsingular affine point. For every n ∈ ℤ: (a) ψₙ(P) = 0 if and only if n·P = O in the group of nonsingular points; (b) φₙ(P) and ψₙ(P) are not both 0 (Ayad's coprimality); (c) if ψₙ(P) ≠ 0 then n·P = (φₙ(P)/ψₙ(P)², ωₙ(P)/ψₙ(P)³).
hypotheses: F a field; P nonsingular. No hypothesis on Δ(W), on n or on the characteristic.
proofSteps: Tau Ceti's zsmul_point_eq_smulEval: the Jacobian coordinates of n·P are the triple (φₙ(P) : ωₙ(P) : ψₙ(P)) for every n, with no hypothesis on the characteristic.

This triple represents a nonsingular Jacobian point, hence is a nonsingular triple. A nonsingular Jacobian triple is the point at infinity exactly when its Z-coordinate vanishes, and then its X-coordinate is nonzero (WeierstrassCurve.Jacobian.X_ne_zero_of_Z_eq_zero); this gives (a) and (b).
(c) A nonsingular Jacobian triple with Z ≠ 0 is the affine point (X/Z², Y/Z³).
acceptance: On y² + y = x³ − x with P = (0, 0) (order ∞), ψ₅(P) = 2 ≠ 0, so 5P = (φ₅/4, ω₅/8) is affine; over 𝔽₂, ψ₅ vanishes and 5P̃ = O.
For the 2-torsion point (0, 0) of y² = x³ − x: ψ₂ = 2y vanishes there and φ₂(P) = 1 ≠ 0.

nodes.title: The zeros of a nondegenerate EDS over a field
nodes.statement: Let K be a field and b, c ∈ K with b ≠ 0, c ≠ 0, d ∈ K. Then {n ∈ ℤ : normEDS b c d n = 0} = rℤ, where r is the order of P = (0, 0) in the group of nonsingular points of E_{b,c,d}(K) (r = 0 if P has infinite order). In particular, for a prime p ∤ bc and an integral normalised EDS W, p | Wₙ if and only if r_p | n, with r_p the order of P mod p (the rank of apparition).
hypotheses: K a field, b ≠ 0, c ≠ 0 in K. For the reading mod p, b, c, d ∈ ℤ and the reductions of b and c are nonzero.
proofSteps: By eds-attached-curve, normEDS b c d n = ψₙ(P) on E_{b,c,d} with P nonsingular.
By division-polynomials-at-a-nonsingular-point (a), ψₙ(P) = 0 iff n·P = O, iff the additive order of P divides n (orderOf_dvd_iff_zpow_eq_one in its additive form addOrderOf_dvd_iff_zsmul_eq_zero).
For p ∤ bc apply this over 𝔽_p to the reduced parameters, using map_normEDS for the reduction ℤ → 𝔽_p.
acceptance: Over 𝔽₂ the sequence 1, 1, −1, 1, 2, … of y² + y = x³ − x reads 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, …: its zeros are 5ℤ, the order of (0, 0) in E(𝔽₂).
Over ℚ, normEDS 2 3 2 = id vanishes only at 0: P has infinite order on the cusp curve.

sources.match: For an elliptic curve over a finite field and a point P of exact order r ≥ 2, gives F_{kr+n}(P) = a^{kn}b^{k²}Fₙ(P) with units a, b (and F_{2k}(P) = 0 when r = 2); since F₀ = 0 and Fₙ(P) ≠ 0 for 0 < n < r, the sequence vanishes exactly at the multiples of r.

nodes.title: The filtration E_k(ℚ_p) for an arbitrary integral Weierstrass equation
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and W a Weierstrass equation with coefficients in ℤ_p, not necessarily minimal, with Δ(W) ≠ 0. For k ≥ 1 let E_k(ℚ_p) = {O} ∪ {(x, y) ∈ W(ℚ_p) : v_p(x) ≤ −2k}. Then each E_k(ℚ_p) is a subgroup of W(ℚ_p), E_k/E_{k+1} ≅ 𝔽_p, and for (x, y) ∈ E_1 the parameter z = −x/y has v_p(z) = −v_p(x)/2. Consequently, for a point Q and a homomorphism n ↦ nQ from ℤ, {n : nQ ∈ E_k} is a subgroup of ℤ.
hypotheses: p prime; W has coefficients in ℤ_p (any integral model); Δ(W) ≠ 0 as in the source, which treats elliptic curves.
proofSteps: The formal group Ê of the Weierstrass equation has coefficients in ℤ_p (it is defined from the a_i universally); for z ∈ pℤ_p the series w(z) converges and z ↦ (z/w(z), −1/w(z)) is an isomorphism Ê(pℤ_p) → E_1(ℚ_p) with v(z) = −v(x)/2 (Streng, Lemma III.2.1; Silverman AEC VII.2.2 for a minimal equation; Tau Ceti's EllipticCurves Layer 1, milestone (iv), plans this identification for an integral model).
Ê(p^kℤ_p) is a subgroup of Ê(pℤ_p), and its image is E_k(ℚ_p); Ê(p^k)/Ê(p^{k+1}) ≅ p^kℤ_p/p^{k+1}ℤ_p ≅ 𝔽_p (Streng, Lemma III.2.3).
The last sentence is the preimage of a subgroup under a homomorphism.

Tau Ceti's EllipticCurves roadmap, Layer 1, plans the elliptic formal group law (milestone (i)), the group Ê(𝔪) over a complete valued field (iii) and the identification Ê(𝔪) ≅ E₁(K) for an integral model (iv); its Layer 4 works from a minimal equation and is not used here. This node adds the finer filtration E_k, k ≥ 1, and its quotients for an arbitrary integral equation (AEC VII, Exercise 7.4, as solved in Streng, Lemma III.2.3).
acceptance: BLRN, Remark 2.5: E: y² + xy = x³ + 4x + 1, P = (15/4, −83/8) ∈ E_1(ℚ₂) with v₂(P) = 1 and v₂(2P) = 4: the quotients E_k/E_{k+1} are 𝔽₂ but E_1(ℚ₂) has 2-torsion, so the valuation is not v(P) + v₂(n) in general.
For W: y² = x³ − p¹²x (not minimal at p), the substitution x = p⁶x′, y = p⁹y′ identifies it with y′² = x′³ − x′, and E_k(W) = E′_{k+3} because v(x) = v(x′) + 6.

nodes.title: Strong divisibility of an integral EDS at primes not dividing W₂W₃
nodes.statement: Let b, c, d ∈ ℤ with b ≠ 0, c ≠ 0, W = normEDS b c d, and p a prime with p ∤ b and p ∤ c, such that E_{b,c,d} is nonsingular (Δ(E_{b,c,d}) ≠ 0). Then for every V ≥ 0 the set {n ∈ ℤ : p^V | Wₙ} is a subgroup of ℤ, and for all m, n ∈ ℤ the p-adic multiplicity satisfies v_p(W_{gcd(m,n)}) = min(v_p(W_m), v_p(W_n)) (with v_p(0) = ∞). For V ≥ 1, p^V | Wₙ holds exactly when nP ∈ E_V(ℚ_p), P = (0, 0) on E_{b,c,d}.
hypotheses: b, c, d ∈ ℤ, bc ≠ 0; p prime, p ∤ bc; Δ(E_{b,c,d}) ≠ 0. No coprimality hypothesis is needed at such primes.
proofSteps: Since p ∤ bc, the coefficients a₁ = (d + b⁴)/(bc), a₂ = c/b², a₃ = b of E = E_{b,c,d} lie in ℤ_(p), P = (0, 0) is integral, and P is nonsingular modulo p because a₃ = b is a p-unit. By eds-attached-curve, Wₙ = ψₙ(P), and φₙ(P), ψₙ(P) ∈ ℤ_(p).

Reduction: the division polynomials have coefficients in ℤ[a₁, …, a₆] (WeierstrassCurve.map_ψ, map_φ), so their values at P reduce to those of the reduced curve at P̃. By division-polynomials-at-a-nonsingular-point (b) over 𝔽_p, p does not divide both φₙ(P) and ψₙ(P).

By division-polynomials-at-a-nonsingular-point (c) over ℚ_p, if Wₙ ≠ 0 then x(nP) = φₙ(P)/ψₙ(P)²; so x(nP) is p-integral when p ∤ Wₙ, and v_p(x(nP)) = −2v_p(Wₙ) when p | Wₙ. If Wₙ = 0 then nP = O. Hence for V ≥ 1, p^V | Wₙ iff nP ∈ E_V(ℚ_p).
By reduction-filtration-of-an-integral-weierstrass-equation (applied to the ℤ_p-model E), {n : nP ∈ E_V} is a subgroup of ℤ; for V = 0 the set is ℤ.
Bezout and the subgroup property give min(v_p W_m, v_p W_n) ≤ v_p W_{gcd(m,n)}; the reverse inequality is divisibility W_{gcd} | W_m, W_n (Tau Ceti isDvdSequence_normEDS).
acceptance: W = normEDS 1 (−1) 1 (curve 37a1), p = 2: v₂(Wₙ) is 0 unless 5 | n, and the multiples of 5 carry the valuations of 5P ∈ E_1(ℚ₂).
W = normEDS 3 2 5, p = 5 (p ∤ bc, 5 | d, Δ ≠ 0): {n : 5 | Wₙ} = 4ℤ and {n : 25 | Wₙ} = 20ℤ within n ≤ 40.

nodes.title: Ward's strong divisibility theorem for elliptic divisibility sequences
nodes.statement: Let b, c, d ∈ ℤ with b ≠ 0 and c ≠ 0, and W = normEDS b c d, the nondegenerate integral EDS with W₀ = 0, W₁ = 1, W₂ = b, W₃ = c, W₄ = db (so W₂ | W₄). Then W is a strong divisibility sequence, gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}| for all m, n ∈ ℤ, if and only if gcd(W₃, W₄) = 1, i.e. c is coprime to db. Equivalently n ↦ |Wₙ| is a strong divisibility sequence on ℕ (Mathlib's Nat.IsStrongDvdSequence).
hypotheses: b, c, d ∈ ℤ with bc ≠ 0 (nondegenerate: W₂W₃ ≠ 0).

The coprimality gcd(W₃, W₄) = 1 is necessary: strong divisibility at (3, 4) says gcd(W₃, W₄) = |W₁| = 1. It cannot be dropped: normEDS 1 (−6) (−6) = 0, 1, 1, −6, −6, 210, −1044, … has gcd(W₃, W₄) = 6.
Absolute values are needed: Wₙ can be negative (W₃ = −1 for the curve 37a1).
proofSteps: Ward's sequences are the normEDS: normEDS b c d satisfies the elliptic net relations (Tau Ceti isEllipticNet_normEDS), hence the EDS recursion, with W₀, …, W₄ = 0, 1, b, c, db; an EDS with W₁ = 1 and W₂W₃ ≠ 0 is determined by W₂, W₃, W₄, and such a triple gives an integral EDS exactly when W₂ | W₄ (Silverman–Stephens, §1, p. 3), so every normalised nondegenerate integral EDS is normEDS b c d for some b, c, d ∈ ℤ with bc ≠ 0.
Necessity: put m = 3, n = 4.
Sufficiency, prime by prime: it suffices that for every prime p, min(v_p W_m, v_p Wₙ) = v_p W_{gcd(m,n)}. The inequality ≥ in the other direction is divisibility (Tau Ceti isDvdSequence_normEDS).
Primes p ∤ bc with Δ(E_{b,c,d}) ≠ 0: eds-strong-divisibility-at-good-primes.

Primes p | bc: by the coprimality, p divides exactly one of b, c, and p ∤ d when p | c. At such primes the point P = (0, 0) can have singular reduction on every integral model of E_{b,c,d}, and the valuations v_p(Wₙ) are then not filtration levels of nP (for b = 1, c = 3, d = 1 and p = 3, where 3 ∤ d + b⁴, no integral model carries P as an integral nonsingular point with Wₙ = ψₙ(P) up to a unit, and v₃(Wₙ) is 0 for 3 ∤ n, 1 for n ≡ 3 (mod 6) and 4 + v₃(n/6) for 6 | n, checked to n = 110 — the sets {n : 3^V | Wₙ} are 3ℤ, 6ℤ, 6ℤ, 6ℤ, 18ℤ, … but the jump from 1 to 4 is not a formal-group pattern). The theorem asserts that the sets {n : p^V | Wₙ} are still subgroups; this case and the singular case Δ(E_{b,c,d}) = 0 are the recorded gap 'Ward's strong divisibility at primes dividing W₂W₃ and for singular attached curves'.
Assemble over all primes: |W_{gcd(m,n)}| and gcd(W_m, Wₙ) have the same p-adic valuation for every p and are nonnegative.
acceptance: normEDS 2 3 2 = id: the theorem reads gcd(m, n) = gcd(m, n).
normEDS 1 (−1) 1 (curve 37a1): W₅ = 2, W₁₀ = −4, W₁₅ = −314, and gcd(W₁₀, W₁₅) = 2 = |W₅|.
normEDS 1 (−6) (−6): gcd(W₃, W₄) = 6 ≠ 1 = |W₁|, so the coprimality hypothesis is sharp.
Numerically: for b ∈ [−6, 6] ∖ {0} and c, d ∈ [−8, 8], c ≠ 0, the 1552 sequences with gcd(c, db) = 1 satisfy gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}| for 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 24.

nodes.title: Formal derivatives of sine and cosine and the Pythagorean identity
nodes.statement: For every commutative ℚ-algebra A, in A⟦X⟧ with Mathlib's PowerSeries.sin A, PowerSeries.cos A and the formal derivative d/dX: (a) d/dX sin = cos; (b) d/dX cos = −sin; (c) sin² + cos² = 1.
hypotheses: A a commutative ring with an algebra structure over ℚ (so that the coefficients ±1/n! exist); no convergence is involved.
proofSteps: (a), (b): compare coefficients with PowerSeries.coeff_derivative: the n-th coefficient of d/dX f is (n + 1)·coeff_{n+1}(f); for sin this is (n + 1)·[n even]·(−1)^{n/2}/(n + 1)! = [n even]·(−1)^{n/2}/n!, the n-th coefficient of cos; for cos it is −[n odd]·(−1)^{(n−1)/2}/n!, that of −sin.

(c): f = sin² + cos² has d/dX f = 2 sin cos − 2 cos sin = 0 by (a), (b) and the Leibniz rule of the derivation, and constant coefficient 0 + 1 = 1; PowerSeries.derivative.ext, whose hypothesis IsAddTorsionFree A holds because A is a ℚ-module (IsAddTorsionFree.of_module_rat, a lemma rather than an instance), gives f = 1.
acceptance: The coefficient of X² of cos is −1/2 and of X³ of sin is −1/6.
These are exactly the formal facts the step 'tan′ = 1 + tan², sec′ = tan·sec' of CA.2/secant-plus-tangent-formal-identity uses.

nodes.title: The Bernoulli series diverges on and beyond |z| = 2π
nodes.statement: (a) For k ≥ 1: |B_{2k}|·(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! = 2ζ(2k) ≥ 2. (b) For z ∈ ℂ with |z| ≥ 2π, the terms B_n zⁿ/n! do not tend to 0, so Σ_n B_n zⁿ/n! is not summable (Mathlib's bernoulli, B₁ = −1/2).
hypotheses: k ≥ 1 in (a); |z| ≥ 2π in (b). This includes the boundary circle, which the analytic theorem's radius statement leaves open.
proofSteps: (a) Mathlib's hasSum_zeta_nat: Σ_{n≥1} 1/n^{2k} = (−1)^{k+1}2^{2k−1}π^{2k}B_{2k}/(2k)!; the left side is ζ(2k) > 1, so (−1)^{k+1}B_{2k} > 0 and |B_{2k}|(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! = 2ζ(2k) ≥ 2 (DLMF (24.9.8) gives the slightly stronger lower bound 2/(1 − 2^{−2k})).
(b) For |z| ≥ 2π, |B_{2k}z^{2k}/(2k)!| ≥ |B_{2k}|(2π)^{2k}/(2k)! ≥ 2 for every k ≥ 1, so the terms do not tend to 0 (Summable.tendsto_atTop_zero, the additive form of Multipliable.tendsto_atTop_one).
acceptance: Together with CA.2/bernoulli-generating-function-on-its-disc this pins the radius at exactly 2π and decides the boundary circle (divergent), which the parent signature not_summable_bernoulli_mul_pow (strict 2π < |z|) leaves open.

sources.match: For n ≥ 1, bounds (−1)^{n+1}B_{2n} below by 2(2n)!/(2π)^{2n} times 1/(1 − 2^{−2n}), and above by the same quantity times 1/(1 − 2^{β−2n}) with β = 2 + log₂(1 − 6/π²) ≈ 0.649 (24.9.9).

nodes.title: The secant-plus-tangent series diverges on and beyond |z| = π/2
nodes.statement: Let e : ℕ → ℚ be any sequence whose odd terms are the tangent numbers in their Bernoulli closed form, e(2n + 1) = (−1)ⁿ2^{2n+2}(2^{2n+2} − 1)B_{2n+2}/(2n + 2) (for the Euler zigzag numbers this is the API item zigzag_odd_eq_bernoulli of CA.2/euler-zigzag-numbers). Then for z ∈ ℂ with |z| ≥ π/2 the terms e(n)zⁿ/n! do not tend to 0, so Σ_n e(n)zⁿ/n! is not summable.
hypotheses: |z| ≥ π/2; only the odd terms of e are constrained.
proofSteps: With k = n + 1, |e(2k − 1)|/(2k − 1)! = 2^{2k}(2^{2k} − 1)|B_{2k}|/(2k)! = 2(2^{2k} − 1)ζ(2k)/π^{2k} by bernoulli-coefficients-do-not-decay (a).
Hence |e(2k − 1)|(π/2)^{2k−1}/(2k − 1)! = (4/π)(1 − 2^{−2k})ζ(2k) ≥ 3/π for every k ≥ 1, and for |z| ≥ π/2 the odd terms have absolute value at least 3/π; the terms do not tend to 0.

sources.match: The lower bound for |B_{2n}| that gives the lower bound for the tangent numbers.
The tangent numbers are the odd-index Euler numbers E_{2n+1}, the coefficients of tan x.

gaps.title: Ward's strong divisibility at primes dividing W₂W₃ and for singular attached curves
gaps.detail: For b, c, d ∈ ℤ with bc ≠ 0 and gcd(c, db) = 1, the subgroup property of {n : p^V | Wₙ}, W = normEDS b c d, is planned only at primes p ∤ bc with Δ(E_{b,c,d}) ≠ 0 (CA.2/eds-strong-divisibility-at-good-primes). Missing: (1) primes p dividing b or c; there the point (0, 0) can have singular reduction on every integral model (b = 1, c = 3, d = 1, p = 3: no integral model carries P as an integral nonsingular point, and v₃(Wₙ) = 1 for n ≡ 3 (mod 6), 4 + v₃(n/6) for 6 | n), so the formal-group argument does not apply; (2) the singular case Δ(E_{b,c,d}) = 0 (sequences satisfying a linear recurrence, e.g. normEDS 2 3 2 = id), where the filtration of the nonsingular points of a singular integral cubic is needed. Sources: Ward, Memoir on elliptic divisibility sequences, Amer. J. Math. 70 (1948), 31–74, proves the theorem by recursion but is not freely available; no public source with a complete proof was found (searched: Silverman arXiv:math/0404412 and his 2007 ICMS slides, Silverman–Stephens math/0402415, Everest–King math/0404124, Everest–McLaren–Ward math/0409540, Bhakta–Loughran–Rydin Myerson–Nakahara 2109.03746, Streng's master's thesis, Stange 0710.1316 and 1108.3051, Silverman–Stange 1001.5303, Verzobio 1906.00632, Xu 2604.05280; Shipsey's and Swart's theses are not online). Numerical evidence: 1552 sequences with b ∈ [−6, 6] ∖ {0}, c, d ∈ [−8, 8], gcd(c, db) = 1 satisfy gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}| for m, n ≤ 24. A wider check by the review: the 3232 sequences with b, c ∈ [−12, 12] ∖ {0}, d ∈ [−6, 6] and gcd(c, db) = 1 satisfy gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}| for 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 32, and in the first range no sequence with gcd(c, db) ≠ 1 is strongly divisible.
